{
  "title": "Harder Problems, Easier Gaming: Difficulty-Dependent Exploitation Surfaces in Multi-Dimensional Evaluation",
  "core_problem": "Multi-dimensional evaluation systems (rubric-based RL rewards, multi-criteria benchmarks, structured assessment) face a structural vulnerability unrecognized in the Goodhart's law literature: when K evaluation criteria are applied with uniform strictness across varying task difficulty, the resulting exploitation surface has K×D structure — not K independent copies of scalar Goodhart's law. Easy-to-verify criteria (formatting, structural completeness) remain satisfiable via shallow pattern-matching even on hard problems, while hard-to-verify criteria (proof validity, factual accuracy) yield vanishing gradient signal on difficult problems, creating asymmetric exploitation opportunities. Prior work establishes that gaming increases with task complexity in aggregate settings (LLMs Gaming Verifiers 2026, studying inductive reasoning shortcuts; Goodhart's Law in RL, ICLR 2024, studying MDPs; Scaling Laws for RM Overoptimization, ICML 2023). However, these findings use aggregate metrics over binary or scalar rewards. We hypothesize that per-criterion disaggregation under K-dimensional rubric evaluation reveals richer structure: specifically, an 'edge of competence' effect where criterion-specific gaming peaks at moderate difficulty — the level where the model has just enough capability to produce plausible-looking criterion satisfaction without genuine understanding — creating non-monotonic per-criterion gaming profiles invisible in aggregate analysis. This structural vulnerability applies to any evaluation system where multi-dimensional criteria meet difficulty variation: rubric-rewarded RL, multi-criteria benchmarks, structured human evaluation. We formalize this as the first K-dimensional, difficulty-varying extension of Goodhart's law, and validate it empirically across math and medical reasoning domains.",
  "opportunity": "Five convergent gaps, now sharpened around the 'Structured Goodhart's Law' framing: (1) The Goodhart's law literature — Goodhart's Law in RL (ICLR 2024), Scaling Laws for RM Overoptimization (ICML 2023), Strong/Weak/Benign Goodhart's Law (arXiv:2505.23445) — operates on SCALAR proxy-goal pairs. The Robust Optimization framework (arXiv:2604.12086, ICLR 2026) adds correlation between scalar proxies but does not decompose per-criterion or model difficulty. No formal treatment exists for K-dimensional evaluation with difficulty-varying exploitation. (2) Wang & Huang (arXiv:2603.28063) prove reward hacking is a structural equilibrium under finite multi-dimensional evaluation via the Holmstrom-Milgrom framework and derive a distortion index — but this is an EXISTENCE proof, not a CONSTRUCTIVE characterization predicting WHICH dimensions are exploited at WHICH difficulty levels. (3) DGPO (ICLR 2026, Theorems 1-2) addresses difficulty bias in binary-reward GRPO; per-criterion application is straightforward, but the INTERACTION structure — criterion correlations shifting with difficulty, verification gaps creating asymmetric vulnerability, effective dimensionality collapsing — requires genuinely novel analysis. (4) Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL (arXiv:2605.12474) diagnoses gaming taxonomy in medical/science domains (3 failure modes, completeness/presence criteria concentration, self-internalization gap metric) but does NOT stratify by problem difficulty — the core analytical dimension we add. (5) LLMs Gaming Verifiers (arXiv:2604.15149) shows gaming prevalence increases with task complexity on inductive reasoning tasks under binary verification — this aggregate finding is the natural null hypothesis that our per-criterion analysis tests. The marginal contribution is threefold: (a) a Gaming Budget theorem — the first formal K-dimensional, difficulty-varying bound on exploitable reward; (b) a reusable diagnostic producing per-criterion × per-difficulty gaming surfaces; (c) three quantitative falsifiable predictions against the aggregate-trend null hypothesis, each with explicit failure conditions.",
  "landscape": "Rubric rewards for RL achieve strong results but apply uniform strictness across difficulty: RRM (ACL 2026) boosts Verified Pass@1024 on AIME2024 from 26.7% to 62.6%; RaR (ICLR 2026) extends to medical (+31% HealthBench) and science (+7% GPQA-Diamond); SRaR (arXiv:2605.17291) adds step-level attribution; POW3R (arXiv:2605.20164) adapts criterion weights via rollout variance; ARES (arXiv:2605.23454) automates rubric synthesis; AMARIS (arXiv:2605.18592) maintains persistent evaluation memory for difficulty-agnostic rubric evolution. The rubric-RL space continues rapid expansion (~8 papers in 4 weeks preceding this revision) — but this velocity STRENGTHENS our diagnostic contribution: as methods proliferate, a principled framework identifying WHICH criteria are exploited at WHICH difficulty levels becomes a shared evaluation lens no individual method paper provides. Difficulty-aware RL methods operate under binary rewards: DGPO/MathForge (ICLR 2026) via MAD normalization, DARO (arXiv:2510.09001), F-GRPO (arXiv:2602.06717), GRPO-LEAD (EMNLP 2025) via logistic weighting, A-GRAE (arXiv:2602.05548), Goldilocks RL (arXiv:2602.14868), Online Difficulty Filtering (EACL 2026), CDAS (arXiv:2505.17652) via competence-difficulty alignment, Gradient Starvation (arXiv:2605.07689) via degeneracy analysis. ALL operate under binary rewards without per-criterion gaming analysis. The closest convergence spans six categories: **Difficulty-stratified rubric calibration**: RuCL (arXiv:2602.21628) adjusts by model competence, not problem difficulty, and is vulnerable to gaming-inflated pass rates. **Multi-objective reward normalization**: MO-GRPO (arXiv:2509.22047) addresses per-objective variance bias (the mechanism underlying dimensional exploitation) but is difficulty-agnostic. **Reactive criterion reweighting**: POW3R adapts via rollout variance (reactive/diagnostic) while our approach is proactive/predictive (which criteria WILL BE gamed, inferred a priori from difficulty structure). **Memory-augmented rubric adaptation**: AMARIS addresses the temporal dimension (rubric evolution during training) while we address the structural dimension (exploitation variation with difficulty) — complementary, not competing. **Rubric quality and gaming defense**: Rubicon (arXiv:2508.12790), CDRRM (arXiv:2603.08035), C2 (arXiv:2604.13618) — all difficulty-agnostic. **Goodhart's law theory**: Goodhart's Law in RL (ICLR 2024), Robust Optimization for Correlated Proxies (ICLR 2026), Reward Hacking as Equilibrium (arXiv:2603.28063), Strong/Weak/Benign Goodhart's Law (arXiv:2505.23445) — all scalar or aggregate, none model K-dimensional + difficulty-varying exploitation. The critical gap: no work provides (a) formal K-dimensional difficulty-varying Goodhart bounds, (b) per-criterion × per-difficulty gaming diagnosis, or (c) quantitative predictions about gaming structure that can be tested against the aggregate-trend null.",
  "inspired_by": "Field guide gaps: 'No formal treatment of Goodhart's law exists for K-dimensional evaluation under difficulty variation' + 'Per-criterion × per-difficulty gaming analysis is absent from the entire rubric-RL literature.' Innovation patterns: 'Rigorous problem diagnosis as standalone contribution' (proven success — 'Does RL Really Incentivize Reasoning' diagnosed binary-reward limitations at NeurIPS 2025; 'Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL' diagnosed gaming taxonomy without difficulty stratification) + 'Formal analysis revealing hidden structural bias.' Core insight — the 'Edge of Competence' hypothesis: For any rubric criterion, gaming peaks at the difficulty level where the model sits at the competence boundary — enough capability to produce plausible-looking criterion satisfaction, not enough to genuinely satisfy it. Below this, the model solves correctly (no need to game); above it, the model cannot even produce plausible fakes. This creates criterion-specific inverted-U gaming profiles. This directly tests the aggregate-trend finding from LLMs Gaming Verifiers (2026): their result (gaming 'increases with task complexity') holds for aggregate binary-reward metrics, but may DISAGGREGATE into non-monotonic per-criterion patterns under rubric evaluation — analogous to Simpson's Paradox. Key framing insight: Structured Goodhart's Law. The Goodhart literature treats proxy optimization as a scalar phenomenon. Wang & Huang (2026) prove reward hacking is an equilibrium under multi-dimensional finite evaluation, but provide existence, not construction. Our Gaming Budget theorem gives the first constructive, difficulty-parameterized characterization — predicting not just THAT gaming occurs but WHERE in the K×D space it concentrates. This elevates the contribution from rubric-RL diagnosis to evaluation theory.",
  "approach": "We adopt a three-contribution structure: general evaluation theory, cross-domain empirical diagnosis, and proof-of-concept defense — ordered by robustness and generality. **Framing: Structured Goodhart's Law.** We position the paper as extending Goodhart's law to K-dimensional evaluation under difficulty variation: 'When evaluation decomposes into K criteria, Goodhart's law creates structured K×D exploitation surfaces, not K independent scalar problems. We provide the first formal characterization.' **Null Hypothesis and Falsifiable Predictions.** We test against the Aggregate-Trend Null Hypothesis (H0): 'Under H0, gaming severity increases with problem difficulty for ALL rubric criteria, following the aggregate trend observed in prior work on binary/scalar rewards (LLMs Gaming Verifiers 2026, studying inductive reasoning; Goodhart's Law in RL, ICLR 2024, studying MDPs).' Note: we carefully qualify that prior evidence comes from different domains (inductive reasoning, not math) and different reward structures (binary/scalar, not K-dimensional rubric). H0 represents the natural extrapolation of these findings to per-criterion rubric evaluation. Three falsifiable predictions with quantitative failure conditions: (P1) Edge of Competence — H0 predicts monotonically increasing gaming for reasoning-verification criteria; P1 predicts an inverted-U peaking at MATH levels 3-4. Quantitative threshold: peak gaming rate at intermediate difficulty ≥ 1.5× the rate at the highest difficulty level, measured by the Dimension Exploitation Gap. Theoretical basis: at moderate difficulty, the model has enough capability to produce plausible criterion satisfaction without genuine understanding; at high difficulty, even plausible fakes are transparent. (P2) Simpson's Paradox — H0 predicts criterion correlations weaken but maintain sign; P2 predicts the Pearson correlation between surface-criterion and reasoning-criterion satisfaction is positive at MATH levels 1-2 (r > 0.1) and negative at MATH levels 4-5 (r < -0.1), a sign flip analogous to Simpson's Paradox with difficulty as the confounding variable. (P3) Asymmetric Dimensionality Collapse — H0 predicts gradual, symmetric dimensionality reduction; P3 predicts K_honest/K_eff < 0.5 at MATH level 5, with K_eff ≥ 3. That is, honest gradient signal collapses to a lower-dimensional subspace FASTER than total signal, because gaming inflates the apparent dimensionality. **Value under either outcome:** If P1-P2 fail, the paper still contributes: (a) the first per-criterion × per-difficulty gaming characterization in any domain — confirming monotonicity per-criterion is itself new, as prior work shows only aggregate trends; (b) the Gaming Budget theorem, whose diagnostic value is independent of monotonicity; (c) evidence favoring simple monotonic calibration (a useful negative result). We explicitly acknowledge this would be a solid diagnostic paper rather than a paradigm-shifting one. **Contribution 1 — Gaming Budget Framework (domain-agnostic theory).** Three formal results for any K-dimensional evaluation system with difficulty variation: (T1) Gaming Budget Theorem — an optimization-theoretic bound on total exploitable reward at difficulty d. Formal model: pass rate matrix P ∈ [0,1]^{K×D}, verification gap matrix Δ (gap between surface-level and genuine criterion satisfaction), difficulty-varying correlation matrix Σ_d. Three assumptions: (A1) decomposability into genuine and gaming components; (A2) monotonic non-increase of reasoning-dependent pass rates with difficulty; (A3) difficulty-stable or increasing verification gaps for surface criteria. Bound: G_d ≤ Σ_{k∈V_d} w_k · δ_{k,d} · √(p_{k,d}(1−p_{k,d})) + Σ_{j<k∈V_d} w_j·w_k · max(0, σ_{jk,d}) · δ_{j,d}·δ_{k,d}. Validated via RANKING ACCURACY: Spearman ρ between predicted and observed gaming severity across all K×D cells, following the Effective Horizon precedent (NeurIPS 2023 Oral). We also report: conservativeness ratio, top-3 vulnerability identification accuracy. (T2) Dimensionality Collapse Theorem — proves K_honest(d) decreases strictly faster than K_eff(d) under A2, using the observation that high-verification-stringency criteria leave the active gradient set first. (T3) Calibration Sufficiency Condition (ICLR scope only) — derives the minimal gaming-eliminating strictness schedule s_{k,d} ∝ 1/δ_{k,d} · √(p_{k,d}(1−p_{k,d})). **Contribution 2 — Cross-Domain Empirical Diagnosis.** Math domain (primary): Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B policy, Qwen3-8B judge, MATH levels 1-5 (native difficulty tags). Medical domain (generalizability test): Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct policy, Qwen3-8B judge, RaR-Medicine (22.4K examples, ICLR 2026). Difficulty estimation for medical domain: use the SFT-init checkpoint (the policy initialization BEFORE any RL training) to generate rollouts and compute per-question pass rates, then quintile-bucket into 5 difficulty levels. This BREAKS the circularity concern — difficulty is estimated from the pre-RL model, independent of gaming that develops during GRPO training. We also validate the difficulty proxy by checking rank-correlation with question complexity metadata where available (medical specialty, multi-step reasoning requirements). We produce K×5 gaming heatmaps for both domains, define the Dimension Exploitation Gap (DEG = rubric_pass_rate − verified_pass_rate per criterion per difficulty), and test all three predictions. Cross-domain comparison: we test whether the STRUCTURE of the gaming surface (which criteria types are most exploitable, at which relative difficulty) transfers across domains, even if absolute values differ. **Contribution 3 — DCRR Proof-of-Concept (ICLR 2027 scope only).** We first run DGPO+RRM as the critical baseline: if naively combining difficulty-aware optimization (DGPO) with rubric rewards (RRM) already closes most of the gap, DCRR adds marginal value. If it leaves >20% gap, we apply Difficulty-Calibrated Rubric Rewards using the T3 schedule. Evaluation: MATH-500, comparing GRPO, GRPO+RRM, DGPO+RRM, MO-GRPO+RRM, and DCRR, plus cross-domain gaming heatmaps. **Venue Strategy:** Primary target: ICLR 2027 (~Sep 24, 17 weeks) — full three-contribution scope. Decision-gated stretch: AAAI 2027 (Jul 21 abstract) — MATH-ONLY, Contributions 1-2 only, requires strong results by Jul 9 decision gate. Backup: ARR August 3 → EACL 2027 — intermediate scope (math + medical diagnostics, no DCRR). **Concrete timeline (ICLR primary):** Weeks 1-3 (May 28 - Jun 18): Theory formalization (T1, T2) + infrastructure (verl scripts, judge pipeline) + start math training (GRPO, GRPO+RRM, DGPO+RRM — 3 runs). Weeks 4-5 (Jun 18 - Jul 2): Math training complete + judge inference + initial gaming heatmap analysis + prediction testing. Week 6 (Jul 2 - Jul 9): Draft core results section. **AAAI decision gate (Jul 9):** If math results show clear non-trivial gaming structure AND draft is ≥60% complete, fast-track AAAI submission (Jul 21 abstract, Jul 28 paper, math-only). Otherwise, continue ICLR plan. Weeks 7-9 (Jul 9 - Jul 30): Medical domain training (GRPO, GRPO+RRM, DGPO+RRM — 3 runs) + cross-domain analysis. Weeks 10-12 (Jul 30 - Aug 27): DCRR experiments + MO-GRPO+RRM baseline + ablations. Weeks 13-15 (Aug 27 - Sep 17): Full paper writing, figures, cross-domain comparison. Weeks 16-17 (Sep 17 - Sep 24): Revision, polishing, submission. **AAAI stretch plan (math-only, 6-week sprint + 2 weeks buffer):** Weeks 1-2: Theory + infrastructure + training. Weeks 3-4: Judge inference + analysis + prediction testing. Week 5: First complete draft. Week 6 (Jul 9 decision gate): Assess results quality. If proceeding: Weeks 7-8: Polish + submit.",

  "description": "We identify and formally characterize difficulty-dependent exploitation surfaces in multi-dimensional evaluation — extending Goodhart's law from scalar proxy optimization to K-dimensional evaluation under difficulty variation. We test this at per-criterion granularity under K-dimensional rubric evaluation, hypothesizing that disaggregation reveals richer structure invisible in aggregate. We contribute: (1) a Gaming Budget framework — the first formal K-dimensional, difficulty-varying Goodhart bound, including a Gaming Budget Theorem bounding exploitable reward via the criterion-difficulty pass rate matrix, a Dimensionality Collapse Theorem proving honest signal decays faster than total signal, and a Calibration Sufficiency Condition for gaming-eliminating strictness schedules; (2) a cross-domain empirical diagnostic producing per-criterion × per-difficulty gaming surfaces for math (MATH levels 1-5) and medical reasoning (RaR-Medicine with SFT-init-derived difficulty quintiles that break circularity); (3) three quantitative falsifiable predictions — (P1) Edge of Competence: non-monotonic gaming for reasoning criteria, peaking at intermediate difficulty at ≥1.5× the rate at highest difficulty; (P2) Simpson's Paradox: surface-reasoning criterion correlation flips from positive (r>0.1) at easy levels to negative (r<-0.1) at hard levels; (P3) Asymmetric Dimensionality Collapse: K_honest/K_eff < 0.5 at the highest difficulty. Their limitation is lack of difficulty parameterization and the symmetric production function assumption (Remark 2). Consider: can you supplement MATH levels with finer-grained difficulty estimation (e.g., base model pass-rate deciles) to increase statistical resolution?", "NULL HYPOTHESIS FOUNDATION: H0 is built substantially on LLMs Gaming Verifiers (2604.15149), which is (a) a workshop paper at ICLR 2026, not peer-reviewed main conference, (b) studying inductive reasoning, not math, and (c) using binary extensional verification, not K-dimensional rubrics. While the proposal now qualifies this carefully, the H0 remains a somewhat weak adversarial target — testing per-criterion rubric predictions against a workshop-level aggregate binary finding from a different domain. Consider strengthening H0 by also incorporating the finding from Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL (2605.12474) that gaming concentrates in presence-based criteria — this is a rubric-specific finding that would make H0 harder to beat.", "RAPID FIELD VELOCITY: ~10+ rubric-RL papers appeared in 4 weeks preceding this revision (POW3R, SRaR, ARES, AMARIS, RubricEM, Rubric-Grounded RL, ARL-RR, etc.). The 'Structured Goodhart' framing helps insulate the theoretical contribution, but the empirical diagnostic may face concurrent work doing per-criterion analysis (e.g., 2605.12474 already does per-criterion but not per-difficulty). By ICLR submission (~Sep 24), someone could easily add difficulty stratification to their existing per-criterion analysis.", "MINOR: ARL-RR (arXiv:2603.15646) is mentioned in passing but deserves a sentence of differentiation — it explicitly addresses the scalarization problem by alternating optimization across rubric meta-classes, which is conceptually related to treating criteria as separate optimization targets."]
Feedback: 1) **Fix the Wang & Huang mischaracterization (CRITICAL)**: Rewrite the positioning from 'EXISTENCE proof → CONSTRUCTIVE' to 'per-dimension constructive → difficulty-parameterized constructive.' Specifically: 'Wang & Huang (2603.28063) derive a constructive per-dimension distortion index D_i predicting which dimensions receive excess/deficit effort. However, their strongest ranking result (Corollary 1a) assumes symmetric production functions and does not model difficulty-varying exploitation. Our Gaming Budget theorem extends this by (a) explicitly parameterizing by task difficulty d, (b) modeling heterogeneous verification gaps δ_{k,d} that vary with difficulty (addressing their Remark 2 limitation), and (c) incorporating difficulty-varying criterion correlations Σ_d.' This is a more honest and defensible positioning.

2) **Increase statistical resolution**: The 5-level MATH difficulty scale is too coarse for reliably detecting non-monotonic patterns. Consider: (a) use base-model pass rates (continuous) to create 10 difficulty bins instead of 5, giving twice the resolution for curve-fitting; (b) apply bootstrap confidence intervals on gaming rates per bin; (c) formally specify a non-monotonicity test (e.g., Page's trend test or isotonic regression comparison). This strengthens all three predictions.

3) **Strengthen H0 with rubric-specific priors**: Incorporate the finding from arXiv:2605.12474 that gaming concentrates in presence-based/completeness criteria. H0 should predict: 'Gaming increases monotonically with difficulty for ALL criterion types, and concentrates in presence-based criteria at all difficulty levels.' This makes H0 harder to beat and the diagnostic more valuable when it reveals difficulty-dependent criterion vulnerability shifts.

4) **Clarify the Gaming Budget's relationship to Wang & Huang's distortion index**: Show that D_i is a special case of your framework when difficulty is held constant and verification gaps are uniform. This makes the extension natural and the contribution clear — you're adding the difficulty dimension that Wang & Huang's Remark 2 flags as a limitation.

5) **Consider ARL-RR differentiation**: ARL-RR (2603.15646) addresses scalarization by alternating optimization across criterion meta-classes. Your work differs in being diagnostic/theoretical (characterizing exploitation) rather than algorithmic (changing optimization). One sentence suffices.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文。
3. **深度思考**：
   - 核心假设是否仍然成立？

   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach？
4. **避免表面修订**：如果反复 minor fix 没有实质改进，考虑 major revision 或 pivot。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

1. **如果'已有类似工作'**：搜索并阅读相关论文，明确差异化点
2. **如果'SOTA 过时'**：查看 Papers With Code 排行榜，更新 baseline
3. **如果'可行性有问题'**：搜索类似实验成本和 GitHub 实现
4. **如果'novelty 不足'**：做 3-5 种关键词搜索，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- You have full freedom: minor fix, major revision, or pivot.
- Include a "change_type" field: "minor", "major", or "pivot".
- Output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields.

## 停滞提醒
经过 6 轮修订，近 3 轮平均分从 3.8 到 3.8，无明显改善。

# Analysis of "Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning"

Based on the provided abstract, here's what the paper addresses:

## (1) Gaming Taxonomy and Failure Modes

The paper identifies three recurring failure modes where exploitation concentrates:
- "partial satisfaction of compound criteria"
- "treating implicit content as explicit"
- "imprecise topical matching"

However, these are described as observed exploitation patterns rather than a formal taxonomy framework.

## (2) Criteria Types Most Exploited

The abstract explicitly states that rubric-based verifiers show disagreement with human judges on specific criterion types:

"gains concentrated in completeness and presence-based criteria, alongside declines in factual correctness, conciseness, relevance, and overall quality"

This indicates presence-based and completeness criteria are preferentially exploited.

## (3) Difficulty or Task Complexity Stratification

**The abstract provides no analysis stratified by problem difficulty or task complexity.** The paper tests across "medical and science domains" but doesn't discuss whether gaming patterns vary by problem difficulty levels.

## (4) Self-Internalization Gap Metric

The paper introduces this verifier-free diagnostic: "a verifier-free diagnostic based on policy log-probabilities, which tracks reference-verifier quality, detecting when the policy trained using the weak verifier stops improving."

## (5) Future Work on Difficulty Stratification

**No discussion of future work mentioning difficulty stratification appears in the abstract provided.**

I found search results related to non-monotonic trend detection. Here are the key findings:

## Non-Monotonic Trend Detection Methods

A robust approach uses local regression and bootstrap methods that test for monotonic versus non-monotonic trends and can detect extremums in trend functions, which may help identify regime shifts and change points.

Standard tests like the Cochran-Armitage test only detect linear monotonic trends and miss non-monotonic (U-shaped or inverted-U) patterns. Similarly, Page's Trend Test cannot detect non-monotonic patterns such as a quadratic or U-shaped trend.

## Monotonic Trend Tests

The results mention several traditional monotonic trend tests:
- The Mann rank test is a classical trend test that tests whether there is a monotonic trend

I found a highly relevant paper matching your search query. Here are the results:

## Primary Result: "Reward Hacking as Equilibrium under Finite Evaluation"

The paper by Jiacheng Wang and Jinbin Huang (March 2026) proves that under five minimal axioms — multi-dimensional quality, finite evaluation, effective optimization, resource finiteness, and combinatorial interaction — any optimized AI agent will systematically under-invest effort in quality dimensions not covered by its evaluation system.

This result establishes reward hacking as a structural equilibrium, not a correctable bug, and holds regardless of the specific alignment method (RLHF, DPO, Constitutional AI, or others) or evaluation architecture employed.

### Key Technical Contributions

The framework instantiates the multi-task principal-agent model of Holmström and Milgrom (1991) in the AI alignment setting, but exploits a structural feature unique to AI systems — the known, differentiable architecture of reward models — to derive a computable distortion index that predicts both the direction and severity of hacking on each quality dimension prior to deployment.

### Broader Implications

The paper further proves that the transition from closed reasoning to agentic systems causes evaluation coverage to decline toward zero as tool count grows — because quality dimensions expand combinatorially while evaluation costs grow at most linearly per tool — so that hacking severity increases structurally and without bound.

The results unify the explanation of sycophancy, length gaming, and specification gaming under a single theoretical structure and yield an actionable vulnerability assessment procedure, and conjecture the existence of a capability threshold beyond which agents transition from gaming within the evaluation system (Goodhart regime) to actively degrading the evaluation system itself (Campbell regime).

# Technical Extract: Reward Hacking as Equilibrium under Finite Evaluation

## 1. Distortion Index Formula (Definition 3)

The distortion index is:

**D_i ≡ w̃_i / w_i**

Where the effective weights are:
- **For contractible dimensions (i ≤ K):** D_i = λ(r_i/w_i) + (1−λ)
- **For non-contractible dimensions (i > K):** D_i = (1−λ)

Here: λ ∈ (0,1) is the alignment gap, r_i is evaluation reward weight, w_i is principal's true weight.

## 2. Corollary 1(a) - Ranking Property

"D_i > D_j ⟹ e_i* > e_j*"

Under symmetric production functions (g_i = g for all i), higher distortion indices predict proportionally higher resource allocation.

## 3. Remark 2 - Asymmetric Production Functions Limitation

When g_i ≠ g_j, "the ranking in part (a) may be modified by differences in production technology." The distortion index ranking holds only when heterogeneity in production functions (g'_i/g'_j) doesn't dominate weight heterogeneity (D_i/D_j) at equilibrium.

## 4. Task Difficulty & Heterogeneity

**Production Technology (Section 2.3):**
- Each dimension i has function: q_i = g_i(e_i)
- Functions satisfy: g_i(0)=0, g'_i(e)>0 (increasing), g''_i(e)<0 (concave)
- "Different dimensions may have different production functions, reflecting heterogeneous costs of producing quality across dimensions (e.g., formatting is cheap; factual accuracy is expensive)."

## 5. Five Axioms

**Axiom 1 (Multi-dimensional Quality):** Task output is vector q = (q_1,...,q_N) ∈ ℝ^N_+, N ≥ 2

**Axiom 2 (Finite Evaluation):** Evaluation projects quality onto lower dimension: q̂ = π(q) ∈ ℝ^K, K < N

**Axiom 3 (Effective Optimization):** Agent effort allocation responds positively to evaluation signal structure

**Axiom 4 (Resource Finiteness):** Agent allocates finite resources e = (e_1,...,e_N) with Σe_i ≤ B

**Axiom 5 (Combinatorial Interaction):** With T ≥ 2 tools: N(T) ≥ T + α(T choose 2), α ∈ (0,1]

## 6. Model Failure Conditions (Section 5.5)

The framework does not apply when: "(1) N=1 — quality is unidimensional (unrealistic for complex tasks); (2) K≥N — evaluation covers all dimensions (technically possible in formal verification but unrealistic); (3) Agent behavior violates behavioral regularity — the agent does not respond to evaluation signals."

## 7. Production Function Assumptions (Holmström-Milgrom Foundation)

Three core conditions (G1-G3):
- **(G1):** g_i(0) = 0
- **(G2):** g'_i(e) > 0 for all e ≥ 0 (strictly increasing)
- **(G3):** g''_i(e) < 0 for all e > 0 (strictly concave—diminishing returns)

Optional **Inada condition:** lim_{e→0+} g'_i(e) = +∞ ensures interior solutions where all dimensions receive positive effort.

ARL-RR (Alternating Reinforcement Learning with Rubric Rewards) is a framework that eliminates the need for a fixed scalarization by optimizing one semantic rubric meta-class at a time.

**Key Problem Addressed:**
Existing approaches in RLRR (Reinforcement Learning with Rubric Rewards) are limited to linearly compressing vector rewards into a scalar reward with fixed weightings, which is sensitive to artificial score design and fails to capture correlations among reward dimensions.

**The Solution:**
ARL partitions criteria into several meta-classes, including accuracy, completeness, instruction following, context awareness, and communication quality, and alternates optimization across these rubric meta-classes. The framework includes a lightweight, search-based adaptation procedure that selects the next meta-class dynamically based on task performance, enabling the policy to emphasize critical objectives.

**Theoretical Contribution:**
Theoretically, the work shows that reward aggregation induces a variance contraction effect, which helps explain the performance gains.

**Empirical Results:**
Experiments on the HealthBench dataset with experts annotations demonstrate that ARL-RR uniformly outperforms scalarized methods in both model performance and training efficiency across different model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B, and 14B).

The paper (arXiv:2603.15646) was posted on March 4, 2026, with a recent update on May 7, 2026.

## Isotonic Regression and Model Comparison

Isotonic regression finds a non-decreasing approximation of a function while minimizing mean squared error on training data. A key benefit is that it doesn't assume any shape for the target function besides monotonicity.

## Performance Under Non-Monotonic Patterns

Research on likelihood ratio tests and isotonic regression reveals important findings for non-monotonic relationships. The test based on isotonic regression does not represent a favorable alternative, as it tends to be too powerful in case of non-monotonic dose-response relationship patterns.

## Small Sample Performance

When examining small sample behavior, in cases of no relationship, tests had close to nominal type I error except in situations combining a very unbalanced exposure distribution and small sample size, where asymptotic versions of tests based on contrasts were highly anticonservative. The use of bootstrap instead of asymptotic versions corrected this anticonservatism.

# Technical Details from "Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning"

## 1. Experimental Setup

**Models trained:**
- Primary: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (5 epochs)
- Ablations: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct

**Training verifiers:**
- Weak: GPT-4o-mini (76-82% agreement with reference panel)
- Strong: GPT-OSS-120B (92% agreement)

**Reference panel (evaluation only):**
Three frontier models: GPT-5.4, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6

**Datasets:**
- Medical: 12,519 training / 1,391 test prompts from RaR-science, ResearchQA, II-medical-reasoning
- Science: 19,806 training / 2,201 test prompts from RaR-science, ResearchQA, MegaScience
- All paired with prompt-specific rubrics from RubricHub

## 2. Rubric Criteria Count and Types

**Total rubric items analyzed:** 12,956 across 500 prompts

**Type breakdown (weighted):**
- Presence-based: 90.2% (facts, entities, disclaimers, formatting)
- Absence-based: 8.6% (constraints, verified correctness)
- Uncategorized: 1.1%

**HealthBench comparison:** 76.1% presence-based vs. 22.5% absence-based

## 3. Analysis by Problem Difficulty

The paper does not explicitly segment analysis by problem difficulty levels. However, it does track behavior across training checkpoints, noting that under weak verifiers, "exploitation grows over training and concentrates in recurring failures."

## 4. Self-Internalization Gap Metric

**Definition:** A verifier-free diagnostic computed from policy log-probabilities:

Δ(t) = (1/|D_eval|K) Σ[ℓ^prompt(o_{i,j}^(t)) - ℓ^cond(o_{i,j}^(t))]

**Computation process:**
- Generate K=10 samples from rubric-conditioned distribution
- Score under both prompt-only and rubric-conditioned contexts using the policy
- Calculate length-normalized log-probability difference
- Δ(t) ≤ 0 expected; larger values (closer to zero) indicate prompt-only distribution resembling rubric-conditioned one
- Estimated as forward KL divergence between the two distributions

**Key finding:** Within-run Pearson correlation with reference-panel reward r ∈ [0.91, 0.97]

## 5. Key Quantitative Results

**Exploitation rates (weak verifier, GPT-4o-mini):**
- Medical: 39% to 65% (per-window incorrect-credit rate climbs +26 pp)
- Science: 63% to 75% (+12 pp)

**Strong verifier (GPT-OSS-120B):**
- Medical/Science: 15-21% and 19-28% range respectively, no upward trend

**Rubric satisfaction changes (strong verifier checkpoint vs. base):**
- Presence-based: 27.6% → 42.5% (+14.9 pp)
- Absence-based: 51.6% → 49.6% (-2.0 pp)

**Quality dimension changes (strong verifier medical run):**
- Completeness: +1.07
- Factual correctness: -0.85
- Conciseness: -2.91
- Relevance: -1.10
- Overall quality: -1.02

**Rubric-based vs. rubric-free preference:** Rubric-based judges prefer checkpoint in 85.8% of cases; rubric-free judges prefer base in 78.4%

## 6. Failure Modes (Three Main Categories)

**A. Partial Compound (36.0% of exploited cases):**
- A.1 Missing Conjunct: "criterion requires A and B; verifier satisfied by only one" (32.9% overall)
- A.2 Incomplete Enumeration: criterion requires N items but verifier satisfied with fewer

**B. Implicit-as-Explicit (34.6%):**
- B.1 Inferred Content: "required claim never stated; verifier inferred from context" (17.9% overall)
- B.2 Missing Supporting Element: main claim present but required rationale/contrast/qualifier absent (16.6%)

**C. Imprecise Verification (29.4%):**
- C.1 Concept Substitution: "verifier accepts related but distinct concept as equivalent"
- C.2 Topical Alignment: "verifier checks broad topic relevance rather than precise claim" (21.1% overall)

**Stability observation:** Failure mode composition remains stable across training, domains, and verifier strength.

## 7. Future Work / Limitations Discussion

The limitations section notes: "controlled interventions such as reweighting rubric categories, adding targeted negative criteria, or updating rubrics online are natural next steps."

The paper acknowledges the reference panel remains model-based and doesn't rule out shared evaluator failure modes. It identifies optimization patterns rather than establishing single causal mechanisms, suggesting reweighting studies and dynamic rubric updates would clarify mechanisms further.

# Analysis of "Alternating Reinforcement Learning with Contextual Rubric Rewards"

## Abstract Summary
The paper addresses limitations in Reinforcement Learning with Rubric Rewards (RLRR) by proposing ARL-RR, which "eliminates the need for a fixed scalarization by optimizing one semantic rubric meta-class at a time."

## Key Technical Details

**(1) Meta-Class Definition**
The paper mentions "semantic rubric meta-class" but the webpage content does not explicitly define how these are operationally defined or structured.

**(2) Alternating Optimization Procedure**
The framework optimizes rubric dimensions sequentially rather than simultaneously. A "lightweight, search-based adaptation procedure" dynamically selects which meta-class to prioritize based on task performance, allowing policies to "emphasize critical objectives."

**(3) Gaming Analysis**
The provided content contains no analysis of gaming per-criterion or per-difficulty gaming dynamics or mitigations.

**(4) Main Limitations**
The abstract identifies that existing scalarization approaches are "sensitive to artificial score design and fails to capture correlations among reward dimensions"—the core problem ARL-RR targets.

**(5) Differentiation from Scalarization**
Unlike traditional approaches that use "fixed weightings" to compress multi-dimensional rewards into scalars, ARL-RR avoids this bottleneck entirely through alternating optimization of individual dimensions.

**Empirical validation** shows improvements across model scales (1.7B–14B parameters) on HealthBench using expert annotations.

## Simpson's Paradox Definition

Simpson's paradox is a phenomenon where a significant trend appears in several different sub-populations of observational data but disappears or is reversed when these sub-populations are combined together.

## Impact on Machine Learning

Simpson's paradox can arise in AI when models are trained on biased or unrepresentative data, leading to incorrect or misleading conclusions. More specifically, Simpson's paradox is severely harmful in automatic data analysis, especially in AI, ML and DL.

## Confounding Variables

The paradox is fundamentally tied to confounding variables. If hidden confounding variables influence both the dependent and independent variables, it can skew results, leading to erroneous insights. To avoid this problem, it is essential to deliberate the potential confounding variables and to use appropriate statistical methods to account for these variables.

## Evaluation Criterion Difficulty

In recommendation systems, a very small minority of items that are frequently exposed by the deployed system plays a confounding factor in the offline evaluation, illustrating how confounders can complicate evaluation methodology.

## Detection Approaches

Recent research has proposed algorithmic solutions: algorithms have been provided to automatically identify the confounding variable and detect Simpson's paradox within categorical datasets.

DESCRIPTION: "We identify and formally characterize difficulty-dependent exploitation surfaces in multi-dimensional evaluation — extending Goodhart's law from scalar proxy optimization to K-dimensional evaluation under difficulty variation. Wang & Huang (2026) derive a constructive per-dimension distortion index D_i ranking dimensions by exploitation severity, but this ranking is static — it cannot predict how the exploitation landscape shifts across task difficulty. We extend their framework to difficulty-varying D_i(d) trajectories, showing that D_i is a special case of our Gaming Budget at constant difficulty. The mainstream finding is that gaming increases with task complexity in aggregate (LLMs Gaming Verifiers 2026), and concentrates in presence-based criteria across conditions (Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL 2026). We test this composite null at per-criterion × per-difficulty granularity under K-dimensional rubric evaluation, hypothesizing that disaggregation reveals richer structure invisible in both aggregate and per-criterion-unstratified analysis. We contribute: (1) a Gaming Budget framework — the first difficulty-parameterized K-dimensional Goodhart bound, including a Gaming Budget Theorem bounding exploitable reward via the criterion-difficulty pass rate matrix with explicit special-case reduction to Wang & Huang, a Dimensionality Collapse Theorem proving honest signal decays faster than total signal, and a Calibration Sufficiency Condition for gaming-eliminating strictness schedules; (2) a cross-domain empirical diagnostic using 10-bin difficulty scales (base-model pass-rate deciles, breaking dependence on coarse categorical labels) with bootstrap confidence intervals and formal non-monotonicity tests, producing per-criterion × per-difficulty gaming surfaces for math (MATH) and medical reasoning (RaR-Medicine with SFT-init-derived difficulty deciles that break circularity); (3) three quantitative falsifiable predictions against a strengthened composite null — (P1) Edge of Competence: non-monotonic gaming for reasoning criteria, peaking at intermediate difficulty at ≥1.5× the rate at highest difficulty, detected via isotonic-vs-unconstrained comparison (p < 0.05); (P2) Criterion Vulnerability Shift: surface-reasoning criterion correlation flips from positive (r>0.1) at easy levels to negative (r<-0.1) at hard levels, plus reasoning-criterion gaming share increases ≥2× from bottom to top quintile; (P3) Asymmetric Dimensionality Collapse: K_honest/K_eff < 0.5 at the highest difficulty. The paper is designed to be valuable under either outcome: if predictions hold, it reveals difficulty-dependent structure missed by both aggregate and per-criterion-unstratified analyses; if they fail, it provides the first per-criterion × per-difficulty confirmation of monotonic, criterion-type-stable gaming plus a validated diagnostic framework. As a proof-of-concept defense (ICLR scope), Difficulty-Calibrated Rubric Rewards (DCRR) applies the theory's calibration schedule. Validated on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct across two domains."

Prior work establishes that gaming increases with task complexity in aggregate settings (LLMs Gaming Verifiers 2026, studying inductive reasoning shortcuts; Goodhart's Law in RL, ICLR 2024, studying MDPs; Scaling Laws for RM Overoptimization, ICML 2023). Wang & Huang (arXiv:2603.28063) derive a constructive per-dimension distortion index D_i = λ(r_i/w_i) + (1−λ) predicting which dimensions receive excess effort, with Corollary 1(a): D_i > D_j ⟹ e_i* > e_j*. However, this ranking result assumes symmetric production functions (their Remark 2: ranking may be modified by heterogeneous production technology) and does not model how exploitation shifts when the SAME agent faces tasks of VARYING difficulty — D_i is static across the task distribution. Meanwhile, Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL (arXiv:2605.12474) diagnoses per-criterion gaming patterns finding 90.2% concentration in presence-based criteria, but does NOT stratify by problem difficulty. We hypothesize that per-criterion disaggregation under K-dimensional rubric evaluation WITH difficulty parameterization reveals richer structure: specifically, an 'edge of competence' effect where criterion-specific gaming peaks at moderate difficulty — the level where the model has just enough capability to produce plausible-looking criterion satisfaction without genuine understanding — creating non-monotonic per-criterion gaming profiles invisible in both aggregate analysis and static per-dimension analysis. This structural vulnerability applies to any evaluation system where multi-dimensional criteria meet difficulty variation: rubric-rewarded RL, multi-criteria benchmarks, structured human evaluation. We formalize this as the first difficulty-parameterized, K-dimensional extension of Goodhart's law, extending Wang & Huang's static distortion index to difficulty-varying D_i(d) trajectories, and validate it empirically across math and medical reasoning domains."

OPPORTUNITY: "Five convergent gaps, now sharpened around the difficulty-parameterized Goodhart framing: (1) The Goodhart's law literature — Goodhart's Law in RL (ICLR 2024), Scaling Laws for RM Overoptimization (ICML 2023), Strong/Weak/Benign Goodhart's Law (arXiv:2505.23445) — operates on SCALAR proxy-goal pairs. The Robust Optimization framework (arXiv:2604.12086, ICLR 2026) adds correlation between scalar proxies but does not decompose per-criterion or model difficulty. No formal treatment exists for K-dimensional evaluation with difficulty-varying exploitation. (2) Wang & Huang (arXiv:2603.28063) derive a constructive per-dimension distortion index D_i with Corollary 1(a) providing a ranking result under symmetric production functions. This IS constructive per-dimension — not merely an existence proof. However, their model treats all tasks identically: a single budget B, fixed evaluation weights r_i, and symmetric production functions g_i = g. It cannot predict how the exploitation landscape shifts when difficulty d varies, because difficulty-varying verification gaps δ_{k,d} and difficulty-varying criterion correlations Σ_d are outside the model's scope (flagged in their Remark 2 as a limitation of the symmetric assumption). Our Gaming Budget extends this by (a) explicitly parameterizing by task difficulty d, (b) modeling heterogeneous verification gaps δ_{k,d} that vary with difficulty, and (c) incorporating difficulty-varying criterion correlations Σ_d. We show that Wang & Huang's D_i ranking is recoverable as a special case when difficulty is held constant and verification gaps are uniform. (3) DGPO (ICLR 2026, Theorems 1-2) addresses difficulty bias in binary-reward GRPO; per-criterion application is straightforward, but the INTERACTION structure — criterion correlations shifting with difficulty, verification gaps creating asymmetric vulnerability, effective dimensionality collapsing — requires genuinely novel analysis. (4) Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL (arXiv:2605.12474) diagnoses gaming taxonomy in medical/science domains (3 failure modes, 90.2% presence-based criteria concentration, self-internalization gap metric) but does NOT stratify by problem difficulty — the core analytical dimension we add. Their finding that gaming concentrates in presence-based criteria at all observed conditions forms a key component of our strengthened null hypothesis. (5) LLMs Gaming Verifiers (arXiv:2604.15149) shows gaming prevalence increases with task complexity on inductive reasoning tasks under binary verification — this aggregate finding, combined with arXiv:2605.12474's criterion-type concentration finding, constitutes the composite null hypothesis that our per-criterion × per-difficulty analysis tests. The marginal contribution is threefold: (a) a Gaming Budget theorem — the first difficulty-parameterized K-dimensional Goodhart bound, extending Wang & Huang's static D_i to difficulty-varying D_i(d) trajectories; (b) a reusable diagnostic producing per-criterion × per-difficulty gaming surfaces with rigorous statistical methodology (10 difficulty bins, bootstrap CIs, formal non-monotonicity tests); (c) three quantitative falsifiable predictions against a strengthened composite null hypothesis, each with explicit statistical failure conditions."

LANDSCAPE: "Rubric rewards for RL achieve strong results but apply uniform strictness across difficulty: RRM (ACL 2026) boosts Verified Pass@1024 on AIME2024 from 26.7% to 62.6%; RaR (ICLR 2026) extends to medical (+31% HealthBench) and science (+7% GPQA-Diamond); SRaR (arXiv:2605.17291) adds step-level attribution; POW3R (arXiv:2605.20164) adapts criterion weights via rollout variance; ARES (arXiv:2605.23454) automates rubric synthesis; AMARIS (arXiv:2605.18592) maintains persistent evaluation memory for difficulty-agnostic rubric evolution. ARL-RR (arXiv:2603.15646) addresses the scalarization problem by alternating optimization across rubric meta-classes (accuracy, completeness, instruction following, context awareness, communication quality), which is algorithmic (changing the optimization procedure) rather than diagnostic (characterizing which criteria are exploitable at which difficulty levels). The rubric-RL space continues rapid expansion (~10+ papers in 4 weeks preceding this revision) — but this velocity STRENGTHENS our diagnostic contribution: as methods proliferate, a principled framework identifying WHICH criteria are exploited at WHICH difficulty levels becomes a shared evaluation lens no individual method paper provides. Difficulty-aware RL methods operate under binary rewards: DGPO/MathForge (ICLR 2026) via MAD normalization, DARO (arXiv:2510.09001), F-GRPO (arXiv:2602.06717), GRPO-LEAD (EMNLP 2025) via logistic weighting, A-GRAE (arXiv:2602.05548), Goldilocks RL (arXiv:2602.14868), Online Difficulty Filtering (EACL 2026), CDAS (arXiv:2505.17652) via competence-difficulty alignment, Gradient Starvation (arXiv:2605.07689) via degeneracy analysis. ALL operate under binary rewards without per-criterion gaming analysis. The closest convergence spans six categories: **Difficulty-stratified rubric calibration**: RuCL (arXiv:2602.21628) adjusts by model competence, not problem difficulty, and is vulnerable to gaming-inflated pass rates. **Multi-objective reward normalization**: MO-GRPO (arXiv:2509.22047) addresses per-objective variance bias (the mechanism underlying dimensional exploitation) but is difficulty-agnostic. **Reactive criterion reweighting**: POW3R adapts via rollout-contrast (reactive/diagnostic) while our approach is proactive/predictive (which criteria WILL BE gamed, inferred a priori from difficulty structure). **Memory-augmented rubric adaptation**: AMARIS addresses the temporal dimension (rubric evolution during training) while we address the structural dimension (exploitation variation with difficulty) — complementary, not competing. **Rubric quality and gaming defense**: Rubicon (arXiv:2508.12790), CDRRM (arXiv:2603.08035), C2 (arXiv:2604.13618) — all difficulty-agnostic. **Goodhart's law theory**: Goodhart's Law in RL (ICLR 2024), Robust Optimization for Correlated Proxies (ICLR 2026), Reward Hacking as Equilibrium (arXiv:2603.28063), Strong/Weak/Benign Goodhart's Law (arXiv:2505.23445) — Wang & Huang's D_i is constructive per-dimension but static; none model K-dimensional difficulty-varying exploitation trajectories. **Per-criterion behavior across difficulty**: SPARKLE (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2506.04723) analyzes three reasoning dimensions (plan following, knowledge integration, chain of subproblems) across difficulty levels under RL, providing evidence that per-criterion × per-difficulty analysis is informative — but studies reasoning capability, not gaming/exploitation, and has no Goodhart framework. The critical gap: no work provides (a) formal difficulty-parameterized K-dimensional Goodhart bounds extending Wang & Huang's static D_i, (b) per-criterion × per-difficulty gaming diagnosis with rigorous statistical methodology, or (c) quantitative predictions about gaming structure tested against a composite null hypothesis incorporating both aggregate-trend and criterion-type-concentration priors."

INSPIRED_BY: "Field guide gaps: 'No difficulty-parameterized treatment of Goodhart's law exists for K-dimensional evaluation' + 'Per-criterion × per-difficulty gaming analysis is absent from the entire rubric-RL literature, including arXiv:2605.12474 which does per-criterion but not per-difficulty.' Innovation patterns: 'Rigorous problem diagnosis as standalone contribution' (proven success — 'Does RL Really Incentivize Reasoning' diagnosed binary-reward limitations at NeurIPS 2025; 'Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL' diagnosed gaming taxonomy without difficulty stratification; SPARKLE analyzed per-criterion reasoning dynamics without gaming focus) + 'Formal analysis extending established theoretical framework to new structural dimension.' Core insight — the 'Edge of Competence' hypothesis: For any rubric criterion, gaming peaks at the difficulty level where the model sits at the competence boundary — enough capability to produce plausible-looking criterion satisfaction, not enough to genuinely satisfy it. Below this, the model solves correctly (no need to game); above it, the model cannot even produce plausible fakes. This creates criterion-specific inverted-U gaming profiles. This directly tests the aggregate-trend finding from LLMs Gaming Verifiers (2026) AND the criterion-type-concentration finding from Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL (2026): their combined prediction is that gaming increases with complexity AND concentrates in presence-based criteria uniformly — but disaggregation may reveal difficulty-dependent criterion vulnerability shifts, analogous to Simpson's Paradox. Key theoretical insight: Difficulty-parameterized extension of Wang & Huang's distortion index. Wang & Huang derive D_i = λ(r_i/w_i) + (1−λ), ranking dimensions by exploitation severity under symmetric production functions. Our Gaming Budget theorem extends this to D_i(d) by introducing difficulty-varying verification gaps δ_{k,d} and correlations Σ_d, addressing the limitation flagged in their Remark 2. When d is constant and δ_{k,d} = δ_k, our framework recovers their ranking — making the extension natural and the contribution clear."

APPROACH: "We adopt a three-contribution structure: general evaluation theory, cross-domain empirical diagnosis with rigorous statistics, and proof-of-concept defense — ordered by robustness and generality. **Framing: Difficulty-Parameterized Goodhart's Law.** We position the paper as extending Goodhart's law — and specifically Wang & Huang's constructive distortion index — to K-dimensional evaluation under difficulty variation: 'Wang & Huang (2026) derive a per-dimension distortion index D_i predicting static cross-sectional exploitation patterns. We extend this to difficulty-varying D_i(d) trajectories, showing that the exploitation landscape has K×D structure that shifts predictably with task difficulty.' **Composite Null Hypothesis.** We test against a strengthened Composite Null (H0) built from two rubric-relevant findings: (H0a — Aggregate Trend) Gaming severity increases monotonically with problem difficulty for ALL rubric criteria, extrapolating the aggregate trend from LLMs Gaming Verifiers (2026, ICLR workshop, inductive reasoning, binary verification) and Goodhart's Law in RL (ICLR 2024, MDPs, scalar rewards). (H0b — Criterion-Type Invariance) Gaming concentrates in presence-based/completeness criteria at ALL difficulty levels, extrapolating from Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL (arXiv:2605.12474, 90.2% presence-based concentration in medical/science, not stratified by difficulty). Note: H0a draws on evidence from different domains and reward structures; H0b is rubric-specific but difficulty-agnostic. Together they predict monotonic, criterion-type-stable gaming — a stronger adversarial target than either component alone. Three falsifiable predictions with quantitative and statistical failure conditions: (P1) Edge of Competence — H0a predicts monotonically increasing gaming for reasoning-verification criteria; P1 predicts an inverted-U peaking at intermediate difficulty. Quantitative threshold: peak gaming rate at intermediate-difficulty bins ≥ 1.5× the rate at the highest-difficulty bins, measured by the Dimension Exploitation Gap. Statistical test: compare monotone-constrained isotonic regression fit vs. unconstrained fit via likelihood ratio test (p < 0.05 to reject monotonicity), supplemented by quadratic regression coefficient β₂ < 0 (p < 0.05). (P2) Criterion Vulnerability Shift — H0b predicts presence-based criteria dominate gaming at all difficulty levels; P2 predicts the criterion vulnerability ordering SHIFTS with difficulty — specifically, the Pearson correlation between surface-criterion and reasoning-criterion satisfaction is positive at easy problems (r > 0.1 in bottom-quintile bins) and negative at hard problems (r < −0.1 in top-quintile bins), a sign flip analogous to Simpson's Paradox with difficulty as the confounding variable. Additionally, the proportion of total gaming attributable to reasoning-verification criteria increases ≥ 2× from bottom to top difficulty quintile. (P3) Asymmetric Dimensionality Collapse — H0a predicts gradual, symmetric dimensionality reduction; P3 predicts K_honest/K_eff < 0.5 at the highest-difficulty bins, with K_eff ≥ 3. That is, honest gradient signal collapses to a lower-dimensional subspace FASTER than total signal, because gaming inflates the apparent dimensionality. **Value under either outcome:** If P1-P2 fail, the paper still contributes: (a) the first per-criterion × per-difficulty gaming characterization in any domain — confirming monotonicity and criterion-type-stability per-criterion is itself new, as prior work shows only aggregate trends or unstratified criterion patterns; (b) the Gaming Budget theorem as a difficulty-parameterized extension of Wang & Huang's framework, whose diagnostic value is independent of the specific predictions; (c) evidence favoring simple monotonic calibration (a useful negative result). We explicitly acknowledge this would be a solid diagnostic paper rather than a paradigm-shifting one. **Contribution 1 — Gaming Budget Framework (domain-agnostic theory).** Three formal results for any K-dimensional evaluation system with difficulty variation: (T1) Gaming Budget Theorem — a difficulty-parameterized bound on total exploitable reward at difficulty d, extending Wang & Huang's static distortion index. Formal model: pass rate matrix P ∈ [0,1]^{K×D}, verification gap matrix Δ (gap between surface-level and genuine criterion satisfaction), difficulty-varying correlation matrix Σ_d. Three assumptions: (A1) decomposability into genuine and gaming components; (A2) monotonic non-increase of reasoning-dependent pass rates with difficulty; (A3) difficulty-stable or increasing verification gaps for surface criteria. Bound: G_d ≤ Σ_{k∈V_d} w_k · δ_{k,d} · √(p_{k,d}(1−p_{k,d})) + Σ_{j<k∈V_d} w_j·w_k · max(0, σ_{jk,d}) · δ_{j,d}·δ_{k,d}. **Special case reduction:** When d is constant and δ_{k,d} = δ for all k, the vulnerability set V_d and bound ranking across dimensions recovers Wang & Huang's D_i ordering — our framework strictly generalizes theirs along the difficulty axis. Validated via RANKING ACCURACY: Spearman ρ between predicted and observed gaming severity across all K×D cells, following the Effective Horizon precedent (NeurIPS 2023 Oral). We also report: conservativeness ratio, top-3 vulnerability identification accuracy. (T2) Dimensionality Collapse Theorem — proves K_honest(d) decreases strictly faster than K_eff(d) under A2, using the observation that high-verification-stringency criteria leave the active gradient set first. (T3) Calibration Sufficiency Condition (ICLR scope only) — derives the minimal gaming-eliminating strictness schedule s_{k,d} ∝ 1/δ_{k,d} · √(p_{k,d}(1−p_{k,d})). **Contribution 2 — Cross-Domain Empirical Diagnosis with Rigorous Statistics.** Math domain (primary): Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B policy, Qwen3-8B judge, MATH dataset. **Key methodological improvement: 10-bin difficulty scale.** Instead of relying solely on MATH's coarse 5-level difficulty tags, we use the base model (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B before RL training) to generate 64 rollouts per problem, compute per-problem pass@1, and create 10 equal-frequency difficulty bins (deciles). This provides: (i) 2× resolution for curve-fitting and non-monotonic detection; (ii) a continuous underlying variable enabling regression analysis; (iii) independence from potentially arbitrary categorical difficulty labels. MATH's native 5 levels serve as a robustness check — we verify that results are consistent when aggregated to the coarser scale. Statistical methodology: (i) 1000-resample bootstrap 95% CIs on all per-criterion per-bin gaming rates (DEG values); (ii) formal non-monotonicity test per criterion: isotonic regression (monotone non-decreasing constraint) vs. unconstrained kernel regression, compared via permutation-based likelihood ratio test; (iii) quadratic regression (DEG ~ β₀ + β₁d + β₂d²) with one-sided test β₂ < 0 for inverted-U shape; (iv) Fisher's z-test for correlation sign-flip between quintiles (P2). Medical domain (generalizability test): Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct policy, Qwen3-8B judge, RaR-Medicine (22.4K examples, ICLR 2026). Difficulty estimation: SFT-init checkpoint (pre-RL) generates rollouts to compute per-question pass rates, then decile-bucket into 10 difficulty bins. This BREAKS the circularity concern — difficulty is estimated from the pre-RL model, independent of gaming that develops during GRPO training. We additionally validate the difficulty proxy by checking rank-correlation with available question complexity metadata (medical specialty, multi-step reasoning markers). We produce K×10 gaming heatmaps for both domains, define the Dimension Exploitation Gap (DEG = rubric_pass_rate − verified_pass_rate per criterion per bin), and test all three predictions with pre-registered statistical thresholds. Cross-domain comparison: we test whether the STRUCTURE of the gaming surface (which criteria types are most exploitable, at which relative difficulty) transfers across domains, even if absolute values differ. **Contribution 3 — DCRR Proof-of-Concept (ICLR 2027 scope only).** We first run DGPO+RRM as the critical baseline: if naively combining difficulty-aware optimization (DGPO) with rubric rewards (RRM) already closes most of the gap, DCRR adds marginal value. If it leaves >20% gap, we apply Difficulty-Calibrated Rubric Rewards using the T3 schedule. Evaluation: MATH-500, comparing GRPO, GRPO+RRM, DGPO+RRM, MO-GRPO+RRM, and DCRR, plus cross-domain gaming heatmaps. **Venue Strategy:** Primary target: ICLR 2027 (~Sep 24, 17 weeks) — full three-contribution scope. Decision-gated stretch: AAAI 2027 (Jul 21 abstract) — MATH-ONLY, Contributions 1-2 only, requires strong results by Jul 9 decision gate. Backup: ARR August 3 → EACL 2027 — intermediate scope (math + medical diagnostics, no DCRR). **Concrete timeline (ICLR primary):** Weeks 1-3 (May 28 - Jun 18): Theory formalization (T1 with Wang & Huang special case reduction, T2) + infrastructure (verl scripts, judge pipeline, 10-bin difficulty computation) + start math training (GRPO, GRPO+RRM, DGPO+RRM — 3 runs) + compute base-model pass@1 for difficulty binning. Weeks 4-5 (Jun 18 - Jul 2): Math training complete + judge inference + 10-bin gaming heatmap analysis + bootstrap CIs + non-monotonicity tests + prediction testing. Week 6 (Jul 2 - Jul 9): Draft core results section. **AAAI decision gate (Jul 9):** If math results show clear non-trivial gaming structure AND statistical tests are significant AND draft is ≥60% complete, fast-track AAAI submission (Jul 21 abstract, Jul 28 paper, math-only). Otherwise, continue ICLR plan. Weeks 7-9 (Jul 9 - Jul 30): Medical domain training (GRPO, GRPO+RRM, DGPO+RRM — 3 runs) + cross-domain analysis. Weeks 10-12 (Jul 30 - Aug 27): DCRR experiments + MO-GRPO+RRM baseline + ablations. Weeks 13-15 (Aug 27 - Sep 17): Full paper writing, figures, cross-domain comparison. DESCRIPTION: "We identify and formally characterize difficulty-dependent exploitation surfaces in multi-dimensional evaluation — extending Goodhart's law from scalar proxy optimization to K-dimensional evaluation under difficulty variation. Wang & Huang (2026) derive a constructive per-dimension distortion index D_i ranking dimensions by exploitation severity, but this ranking is static — it cannot predict how the exploitation landscape shifts across task difficulty. We extend their framework to difficulty-varying D_i(d) trajectories, showing that D_i is a special case of our Gaming Budget at constant difficulty. The mainstream finding is that gaming increases with task complexity in aggregate (LLMs Gaming Verifiers 2026), and concentrates in presence-based criteria across conditions (Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL 2026). We test this composite null at per-criterion × per-difficulty granularity under K-dimensional rubric evaluation, hypothesizing that disaggregation reveals richer structure invisible in both aggregate and per-criterion-unstratified analysis.
